nodes.title: Step 1: Check Your Eligibility
nodes.description: Before anything else, confirm you have the legal right to vote in your jurisdiction.
steps: Confirm you meet the minimum age requirement (typically 18 years old)
Verify your citizenship or residency status qualifies you to vote
Check that you are not disqualified by any court order or legal restriction
nodes.why_it_matters: Voting is a fundamental civic right — but it has legal requirements. Knowing your eligibility protects you from wasted effort and ensures your vote counts.

region_notes.USA: Age 18+. U.S. citizens only. Some states restore voting rights to former felons — check your state's rules.
region_notes.UK: Age 18+ (16+ in Scotland/Wales for some elections). British, Irish, or qualifying Commonwealth citizen.
region_notes.India: Age 18+. Indian citizen. Name must appear on Electoral Roll.

nodes.title: Step 2: Register to Vote
nodes.description: Registration puts your name on the official voter roll — without it, you cannot vote.
steps: Locate your official voter registration portal (national or state/local authority website)
Complete the registration form with your legal name, address, and date of birth
Submit before the registration deadline — deadlines vary significantly by region
nodes.why_it_matters: You can be fully eligible but still unable to vote if you are not registered. Registration is the gateway — it is how the election authority knows you exist as a voter.

region_notes.USA: Register at vote.gov or your state's election website. Deadlines vary — some states allow same-day registration. Check your state's specific rules.
region_notes.UK: Register at gov.uk/register-to-vote. Deadline is typically 12 working days before an election. Individual Electoral Registration (IER) system.
region_notes.India: Register via voters.eci.gov.in using Form 6. The ECI conducts annual summary revisions. You can register year-round.

nodes.title: Step 3: Get Your Voter ID / Documents
nodes.description: Many jurisdictions require you to bring identification to vote. Know what you need in advance.
steps: Find out what form of ID is accepted at polling stations in your region
If you lack the required ID, apply for a voter ID card through your electoral authority
Keep your voter registration confirmation or polling card — you may need it on Election Day
nodes.why_it_matters: Arriving without the right ID can mean you cannot vote, even if you are fully registered. Preparation on this step eliminates a very fixable problem.

region_notes.USA: ID requirements vary by state — some require photo ID, others only need a signature match. Check your state's voter ID law.
region_notes.UK: Photo ID is now required in Great Britain (since 2023). Accepted: passport, driving licence, or free Voter Authority Certificate from your council.
region_notes.India: Voter ID card (EPIC) is the primary ID. Also accepted: Aadhaar, passport, driving licence, PAN card, and several others.

nodes.title: Step 4: Find Your Polling Station
nodes.description: You must vote at your assigned polling station — you generally cannot vote at a different one.
steps: Look up your assigned polling station on your electoral authority's website using your registered address
Note the station's address and opening/closing hours
Plan your route and check for accessibility if needed
nodes.why_it_matters: Showing up at the wrong polling station wastes your trip and may mean you miss the chance to vote. Knowing your station in advance removes all uncertainty on Election Day.

region_notes.USA: Use vote.gov or your state's lookup tool. Polling hours vary by state, typically 6am–8pm local time.
region_notes.UK: Polling cards are sent to your registered address. Stations typically open 7am–10pm on election day.
region_notes.India: Check your Voter Information Slip or voters.eci.gov.in. Polling typically runs 7am–6pm, sometimes extended in some constituencies.

nodes.title: Step 5: Understand Your Ballot
nodes.description: Know who and what you will be voting for before you enter the polling booth.
steps: Research the candidates and parties on your ballot — look up their platforms
Understand the voting method used (first-past-the-post, ranked choice, proportional, etc.)
If there are referendums or propositions, read official summaries from your electoral authority
nodes.why_it_matters: An informed vote is a powerful vote. Understanding your ballot before you arrive means you are not guessing under pressure in the booth.

region_notes.USA: Presidential elections use Electoral College; many races use First-Past-The-Post. Some states use ranked-choice voting. Sample ballots often available online.
region_notes.UK: First-Past-The-Post for general elections. In some devolved elections (Scotland, Wales) proportional representation is used.
region_notes.India: First-Past-The-Post for Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections. Voting is on EVMs — candidates listed with party symbols.

nodes.title: Step 6: Arrive at Your Polling Station
nodes.description: Election Day has arrived. Here is what to do when you get there.
steps: Bring your required ID and any voter registration confirmation or polling card
Arrive with enough time — polling stations can have queues, especially in the morning and after work hours
If you are in the queue before closing time, you have the right to vote — do not leave
nodes.why_it_matters: The logistics of Election Day are simple, but easy to get wrong. Getting there prepared and on time is the difference between your vote counting and being left out.

region_notes.USA: If you are in line when polls close, you have the right to vote. Some states have long early voting periods.
region_notes.UK: Polls close at 10pm. Any voter in the queue at 10pm can vote. You do not need your polling card — it just speeds up the process.
region_notes.India: Carry your Voter ID or any approved alternate ID. If your name is on the roll, you can vote. Queues can be very long in populous constituencies.

nodes.title: Step 7: Check In at the Polling Station
nodes.description: When you enter, polling staff will verify your identity and find you on the voter roll.
steps: Present your ID to the polling officer at the check-in desk
The officer will find your name on the electoral register and mark you as attending
You will receive your official ballot paper or be directed to a voting machine
nodes.why_it_matters: The check-in process is how election authorities prevent fraud and ensure one person = one vote. It is quick and straightforward — polling officers are trained to help.

region_notes.USA: Show your ID (if required by your state) and state your name/address. You may be asked to sign a poll book.
region_notes.UK: Show your photo ID. The clerk will cross your name off the register and hand you a ballot paper.
region_notes.India: Show your Voter ID or approved alternative. The presiding officer checks the roll and applies indelible ink to your finger to prevent double voting.

nodes.title: Step 8: Cast Your Vote
nodes.description: This is the moment. Mark your ballot correctly and submit it.
steps: Go to the private voting booth — your vote is secret, no one can see what you mark
Mark your ballot clearly according to the instructions (tick, cross, number, or press a button on EVM)
Follow the submission process: fold and place paper ballot in the sealed box, or confirm on the EVM
nodes.why_it_matters: A spoiled or incorrectly marked ballot may not be counted. Taking 60 seconds to mark it correctly is the most important action you take today.

region_notes.USA: Methods vary: paper ballot, optical scan, or touch screen depending on your county. Follow the instructions on the ballot.
region_notes.UK: Put a single X in the box next to your chosen candidate. Fold the paper and place it in the ballot box. Any other marking may spoil your ballot.
region_notes.India: Press the blue button next to your chosen candidate's name and symbol on the EVM. A beep confirms your vote. The VVPAT shows a paper confirmation.

nodes.title: Step 9: Votes Are Counted
nodes.description: After polls close, a rigorous counting process begins under official supervision.
steps: Ballot boxes are sealed, transported, and opened only at official counting centers under strict security
Votes are counted by electoral officials — candidates or their agents can observe the count
Results are verified, cross-checked, and any disputed ballots are reviewed by returning officers
nodes.why_it_matters: The counting process is designed to be transparent and tamper-proof. Understanding it builds confidence that your vote was counted correctly and fairly.

region_notes.USA: Counting timelines vary by state. Mail-in ballots may take days to process. Networks project winners, but official certification takes weeks.
region_notes.UK: Counting often begins immediately after polls close at 10pm. Results for most constituencies are announced overnight.
region_notes.India: Counting day is a separate official day, usually 1–2 weeks after the last polling phase. EVM results are announced by the Returning Officer.

nodes.title: Step 10: Results Are Declared
nodes.description: Official results are announced and a winner is formally declared.
steps: The Returning Officer or equivalent authority officially announces the winner in each constituency/race
Final results are certified and published on the official electoral authority website
The winning party or candidate begins the process of forming a government or taking office
nodes.why_it_matters: Understanding how results are officially declared — versus projected by media — prevents misinformation. Official results are what legally matter.

region_notes.USA: States certify results within weeks. The Electoral College meets in December. Inauguration Day is January 20th. Media projections are not official.
region_notes.UK: Most results declared overnight. Official gazette publication follows. The PM is appointed by the monarch once a majority is clear.
region_notes.India: ECI declares results on counting day. The President invites the largest party/coalition leader to form the government.

nodes.title: Step 11: Disputes and Appeals
nodes.description: If you believe there was an irregularity, there are official processes to raise concerns.
steps: Contact your local electoral authority or returning officer to report a specific concern
Election petitions can be filed in court — there are strict deadlines (typically 21–30 days post-result)
Recounts can be requested if the margin is very narrow — the process is formal and supervised
nodes.why_it_matters: Democracy depends on trust in the process. Legitimate dispute channels exist for good reason. However, baseless claims undermine democracy — always rely on official evidence.

region_notes.USA: Recounts can be triggered automatically (narrow margins) or requested. Legal challenges go to state courts then federal if applicable.
region_notes.UK: Election petitions must be filed within 21 days of the result. They are heard by an Election Court (two High Court judges).
region_notes.India: Election petitions filed in High Court within 45 days. The ECI also has powers to countermand elections in cases of serious malpractice.

nodes.title: Step 12: Your Ongoing Civic Role
nodes.description: Voting is the start of civic engagement, not the end of it.
steps: Track the actions of your elected representative — hold them accountable to their promises
Engage with your local government: attend town halls, write to your MP/representative, join civic groups
Prepare for the next election: keep your registration up to date when you move or change circumstances
nodes.why_it_matters: Democracy is not a one-day event. Between elections, engaged citizens drive accountability. Your voice matters beyond the ballot box.

region_notes.USA: Contact your Representatives and Senators via congress.gov. Local elections happen frequently — stay registered and engaged.
region_notes.UK: Write to your MP via writetothem.com. Local council elections and by-elections occur regularly.
region_notes.India: Contact your MP via the Lok Sabha website. RTI (Right to Information) applications are a powerful civic tool.

faqs.question: Can I vote if I am not registered?
faqs.answer: In most countries, no — you must be on the official electoral register before you can vote. Some places allow same-day registration, but this is the exception, not the rule. Register early to be safe.

faqs.question: What if I spoil my ballot?
faqs.answer: A spoiled ballot (incorrectly marked, torn, or defaced) is generally not counted. In most systems, you can ask for a replacement ballot if you have not yet submitted it. Once submitted, it cannot be retrieved.

faqs.question: Is my vote really secret?
faqs.answer: Yes. Ballot papers and EVMs are designed to make your specific vote untraceable to you personally. The secret ballot is a cornerstone of free and fair elections in all major democracies.

faqs.question: How long does counting take?
faqs.answer: It depends on the country and scale of the election. UK results often come overnight. US results can take days due to mail-in ballots. Indian results are announced on a dedicated counting day, weeks after polling.

faqs.question: What if I cannot get to the polling station?
faqs.answer: Most systems offer alternatives: postal/absentee voting, proxy voting (someone votes on your behalf), or accessible voting facilities. Contact your electoral authority well in advance — deadlines apply.

faqs.question: Do I have to vote for all positions on the ballot?
faqs.answer: Generally you can choose to vote in only some races — this is called an 'undervote.' Your vote in the races you participate in will still count. A completely blank ballot would be considered spoiled.
